sources.claim: Heapsort builds a max heap and repeatedly moves the root to the shrinking sorted suffix in O(n log n) time and O(1) auxiliary array space.

canonicalExplanation.summary: **Heapsort** sorts an array in place in two phases. **Build** a **max-heap** from the whole array in O(n). Then **repeat**: swap the root (the largest item) with the **last item of the heap part**, shrink the heap by one so that item is now in the **sorted suffix**, and **sift down** the new root **within the smaller heap only**. After n - 1 rounds the array is sorted ascending. It's always **O(n log n)**, uses **O(1)** extra array space, but is **not stable** and tends to be slower in practice than a good quicksort because it jumps around memory.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
An embedded scoreboard with very little memory must sort 10,000 scores with a guaranteed worst-case time. Merge sort needs extra memory, quicksort can hit O(n²). The first heapsort attempt sifts down over the whole array after each swap and pulls sorted items back into the heap. After each root swap, sift-down restores heap order only in the unsorted prefix. In this lesson you'll implement or trace heapsort and compare it with merge sort and quicksort.

sections.heading: The invariant: heap prefix, sorted suffix
sections.body:
```python
def sift_down_max(a, i, size):          # heap is a[:size].
    while True:
        largest, l, r = i, 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
        if l < size and a[l] > a[largest]: largest = l
        if r < size and a[r] > a[largest]: largest = r
        if largest == i:
            return
        a[i], a[largest] = a[largest], a[i]
        i = largest

def heapsort(a):                         # O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):  # build a max-heap, O(n).
        sift_down_max(a, i, n)
    for end in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
        # Invariant: a[:end+1] is a max-heap; a[end+1:] is sorted.
        a[0], a[end] = a[end], a[0]      # move the max into the sorted suffix.
        sift_down_max(a, 0, end)         # repair the heap in a[:end] only.

scores = [70, 95, 60, 88, 75]
heapsort(scores)
print(scores)                             # [60, 70, 75, 88, 95]
```

| Sort | Worst time | Extra space | Stable |
|---|---|---|---|
| heapsort. | O(n log n). | O(1). | no. |
| merge sort. | O(n log n). | O(n). | yes. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why a max-heap to sort ascending?", "answer": "Each round moves the largest remaining item to the end of the unsorted part, so the sorted suffix grows from the back in ascending order."}
```

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Heapsort is stable because equal values keep heap insertion order.
misconceptions.correction: Heap operations swap items across long distances, so equal items can change relative order. Heapsort is not stable; use a stable sort when ties must keep their order.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why might Chen end up before Asha?

analogy.example: Heapsort is like **a talent show with one stage**: the best remaining act (root) is called forward and placed at the end of the "finished" line, then the others reshuffle so the next best is on stage. The finished line never rejoins the show.
usefulFor: remembering max to the back, heap shrinks
boundary = the edge of the stage
limitations: Talent shows keep ties by sign-up time; heapsort doesn't.
Every round is quick: one path of reshuffling, O(log n).

artifact: swap 95 to end; sift in a[:4]
